clinicalPearls: Bilirubin is the terminal product of heme catabolism, with roughly 70-90% derived from breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent red cells; hepatic handling involves four linked steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases (ligandins), conjugation by UGT1A1, and canalicular excretion (Harrison 22e p.2637-2638).

Conjugation by UGT1A1 adds one or two glucuronic acid moieties, disrupting internal hydrogen bonding so the resulting glucuronides become water-soluble; conjugation is obligatory for biliary excretion (Harrison 22e p.2638).

Unconjugated bilirubin is too tightly albumin-bound to be filtered and does not appear in urine, whereas conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin is readily filtered, so bilirubinuria indicates a conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia; the kidney acts as an overflow valve so renal failure can amplify jaundice in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Harrison 22e p.2638).

Isolated hemolysis in an otherwise healthy person produces a purely unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with direct fraction <=15% of total; because marrow erythropoiesis can rise only about eightfold, hemolysis alone rarely sustains a bilirubin above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL), so higher values imply concomitant hepatic dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2638-2639).

Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign cause of mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <51 micromol/L, <3 mg/dL) with normal liver tests and histology; levels rise with fasting, stress, fatigue, alcohol, and intercurrent illness and fall with caloric intake or enzyme inducers (Harrison 22e p.2640).

Crigler-Najjar type I shows extreme lifelong unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL) with essentially absent UGT1A1 activity, no response to phenobarbital, and high kernicterus risk; type II has lower levels, detectable enzyme, pigmented bile, and a >25% bilirubin fall with phenobarbital (Harrison 22e p.2639-2640).

Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign, autosomal recessive predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (typically 34-85 micromol/L) caused by mutation of the canalicular transporter MRP2 (ABCC2); the liver is grossly black from lysosomal pigment and urinary coproporphyrin is >=80% isomer I despite a normal total (Harrison 22e p.2640-2641).

Rotor syndrome resembles Dubin-Johnson clinically (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria) but the liver is normal in color, the gallbladder is visualized on oral cholecystography, and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly increased with isomer I usually <70%; it results from combined deficiency of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (Harrison 22e p.2641-2642).

Most neonates develop mild physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia between days 2 and 5 (peak typically <85-170 micromol/L, 5-10 mg/dL) due to low UGT1A1 and enterohepatic recycling, resolving within about 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2639).

A rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin, or absolute levels above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL), risks bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) as pigment crosses an immature blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia (Harrison 22e p.2639).

Acquired liver disease (acute hepatitis, common bile duct stone) generally produces a mixed conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and serum levels or fractions cannot reliably distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2640).

Gilbert syndrome impairs glucuronidation of the irinotecan (CPT-11) active metabolite SN-38, predisposing to severe diarrhea and myelosuppression; the HIV protease inhibitors indinavir and atazanavir inhibit UGT1A1 and worsen hyperbilirubinemia, most markedly in preexisting Gilbert syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2640).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bilirubin, the end product of heme degradation (chiefly from senescent erythrocyte hemoglobin), circulates tightly bound to albumin and is processed by hepatocytes in four steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases, conjugation with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1 (the physiologically critical isoform encoded by exon A1 plus shared exons 2-5 of the UGT1 gene complex on chromosome 2), and ATP-dependent canalicular excretion of mono- and diglucuronides via MRP2. A portion of glucuronides is also exported into the portal circulation by MRP3 and recaptured by sinusoidal OATP1B1/OATP1B3. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from overproduction (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, resorption of large hematomas/infarcts), decreased hepatic uptake (drugs such as rifampin, novobiocin; contributory in Gilbert syndrome), or impaired conjugation (neonatal immaturity, breast-milk jaundice, drug inhibition of UGT1A1, and hereditary UGT1A1 defects of Crigler-Najjar I/II and Gilbert syndrome). Gilbert syndrome most often reflects a homozygous extra TA insertion (A[TA]7TAA rather than A[TA]6TAA) in the UGT1A1 promoter reducing enzyme expression; Crigler-Najjar reflects coding/structural UGT1 mutations causing absent (type I) or markedly reduced (type II) activity. Predominantly conjugated familial hyperbilirubinemias result from defective canalicular excretion: Dubin-Johnson from MRP2 (ABCC2) mutation and Rotor from combined OATP1B1/OATP1B3 deficiency impairing reuptake of refluxed conjugated bilirubin.

harrison.prognosis: Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes are benign with normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease. Crigler-Najjar type I carries a grave prognosis: before phototherapy most patients died of kernicterus in infancy or early childhood, and even survivors developed bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction, with early liver transplantation the best means to prevent brain injury and death. Crigler-Najjar type II is far less often complicated by kernicterus and is generally compatible with normal life, though intercurrent illness, fasting, or low albumin can precipitate dangerous bilirubin elevations. BRIC is benign and does not cause cirrhosis, whereas PFIC progresses to end-stage liver disease in childhood.
pitfalls: Assuming hemolysis alone explains a markedly elevated bilirubin; sustained levels above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) imply coexisting hepatic dysfunction
Using serum bilirubin levels or conjugated/unconjugated proportions to differentiate intrahepatic from extrahepatic causes of jaundice, which is not reliable
Overdiagnosing Gilbert syndrome from a single value, since levels fluctuate widely and at least 25% of patients show transiently normal bilirubin on follow-up
Male predominance in Gilbert syndrome may be artifactual, reflecting use of male-derived reference ranges
Mistaking the first episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis for acute viral hepatitis
Prescribing drugs cleared by glucuronidation (notably irinotecan) without caution in Gilbert syndrome given risk of severe toxicity
harrison.severityClassification: Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia forms a severity continuum by residual UGT1A1 activity: Crigler-Najjar type I (activity absent; bilirubin ~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL; no phenobarbital response; usual kernicterus), Crigler-Najjar type II (reduced activity, typically <=10% of normal; bilirubin ~100-430 micromol/L, 6-25 mg/dL; >25% phenobarbital response; rare kernicterus), and Gilbert syndrome (activity ~10-35% of normal; bilirubin usually <=70 micromol/L, 4 mg/dL absent fasting/hemolysis; normal histology). Familial conjugated hyperbilirubinemias of canalicular function (Dubin-Johnson, Rotor) are benign, distinguished from the progressive cholestatic disorders BRIC (episodic, non-progressive) and PFIC (progressive to end-stage liver disease).
management: Reassurance without treatment for the benign syndromes (Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson and Rotor), advising avoidance of precipitants such as fasting, dehydration and intercurrent-illness stress in Gilbert syndrome
Induce residual UGT1A1 activity with phenobarbital in Crigler-Najjar type II to lower bilirubin
In Crigler-Najjar type I prevent kernicterus with intensive phototherapy and exchange transfusion for acute rises, as the enzyme is absent and phenobarbital is ineffective
Reserve liver transplantation as the definitive cure for Crigler-Najjar type I, ideally before neurological injury develops
Avoid drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin and, in Dubin-Johnson, oral oestrogens that can precipitate jaundice
Monitor unconjugated bilirubin and neurological status, particularly in neonates and during intercurrent illness, given kernicterus risk in Crigler-Najjar
Offer genetic counselling, as Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson and Rotor are autosomal recessive and Gilbert relates to a UGT1A1 promoter polymorphism
